{{Short description|Canadian-American mathematician (1921–2017)}}
'''Albert "Tommy" Wilansky''' (13 September 1921, [[St. John's, Newfoundland]] – 3 July 2017, [[Bethlehem, Pennsylvania]]) was a Canadian-American mathematician, known for introducing [[Smith number]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Wilansky, A.|title=Smith numbers|journal=Two-Year College Mathematics Journal|volume=13|year=1982|issue=1 |page=21|doi=10.2307/3026531|jstor=3026531}}</ref><ref name=obit>{{cite news|title=Obituary. Albert Wilansky|newspaper=The Morning Call|location=Allentown, Pennsylvania|date=July 11, 2017|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/mcall/obituary.aspx?n=albert-wilansky&pid=186052058&fhid=6123}}</ref>

==Biography==
Wilansky was educated as an undergraduate at [[Dalhousie University]], where he received an M.A. in mathematics in 1944. From 1944 to 1947 he was a graduate student at Brown University.<ref name=EPADEL>{{cite web|author=Zitarelli, David E.|title=EPADEL: A Sesquicentennial History, 1926–2000|url=https://www.personal.psu.edu/ecb5/EPaDel/Zittarelli/EPL0_Intro.html}} (See personal profile of Albert Wilansky in Chapter 6.)</ref> In 1947 he received his Ph.D. with advisor [[Clarence Raymond Adams]] and dissertation ''An application of Banach linear functionals to the theory of summability''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=4341|name=Albert "Tommy" Wilansky}}</ref>

From 1948 until his official retirement in 1992, Wilansky was a faculty member of the mathematics department of [[Lehigh University]].<ref name=EPADEL/>

{{blockquote|He was the university’s Distinguished Professor of Mathematics for the final 14 years of his tenure. During his 44 years at Lehigh he was a Fulbright visiting professor several times, at universities in Reading (1972–1973), London (1973), Tel Aviv (1981), and Berne (1981). Outside of academia he was a consultant for the [[Frankford Arsenal]] for the year 1957–1958.<ref name=EPADEL/>}}

Wilansky did research in analysis, specializing in summability theory, linear topological spaces, Banach algebras, and functional analysis.<ref name=EPADEL/> He was the author of several books and the author or co-author of more than 80 articles. He lectured at over 50 different universities.<ref name=obit/> In 1969 he received the [[Mathematical Association of America]]'s [[Lester R. Ford Award]] for his 1968 article ''Spectral Decomposition of Matrices for High School Students''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Spectral Decomposition of Matrices for High School Students|website=Mathematical Association of America|url=https://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/spectral-decomposition-of-matrices-for-high-school-students}} (with link to PDF of article, which was published in ''[[Mathematics Magazine]]'' )</ref> (The 1969 award was also given individually to 5 other mathematicians.)

Wilansky was married to his first wife from 1947 until her death in 1969. They had two daughters. He had three step-daughters from his second marriage.

{{blockquote|He was a professional musician for a brief time as a young man and continued playing piano and clarinet and writing songs, often with his wives and daughters.<ref name=obit/>}}
